blocks.text: MUSEUM RECORDS · OPEN LICENCES · NAMED OBJECTS
Not a list of proofs. A list of objects, and of the museums that have them.

Every record on these pages was taken from a museum or archive that publishes its catalogue openly, and every photograph was copied only because its own source stated an open licence. Each object carries the museum's own number, its date as the museum records it, where it was found, and — where our archaeology catalogue has an audited row for it — what that row says the object does and does not support.
One photograph from each of the collections that has one. Every picture on this site but these is our own drawing; these are the objects.
Photographs are shown at the museums' own open licences, each credited on its own object. No museum here endorses a biblical reading of its objects.

Two different relationships, never added together: the collections these records were fetched from, and the institutions those records name as holding the object. One tablet is both a catalogue record and a British Museum object.
OPEN COLLECTIONS THESE RECORDS CAME FROM
Eight museums, archives and catalogues that publish their records openly. Everything on this page was fetched from one of them.
The Met publishes its whole collection catalogue as open data, and marks which objects are free of copyright. It is the largest single source here by a wide margin.

Cleveland's open-access API let the museum itself filter by date, so every record here was returned as falling inside the biblical period. Most of its photographs are of objects from elsewhere in the ancient world, and the page…

The Art Institute's catalogue is open and names a findspot for almost every object. Its image server refuses a non-browser client, so the picture addresses and licences are recorded and no file was copied.

The Smithsonian's open-access search covers every one of its museums. Its holdings from the biblical world turned out to be thin: a documented demo key allows about thirty calls an hour, and of the records it returned only a…

Europeana is not a museum. It gathers the catalogues of European institutions and publishes their descriptions under a single open licence, while each item keeps its own rights statement. The institutions behind these records…

Wikidata holds no object. It is how the named objects were resolved: each one was looked up once, checked against its expected name, and rejected if it turned out to be a person or a modern paper. The photographs come from…

The Open Richly Annotated Cuneiform Corpus publishes edited Assyrian and Babylonian texts project by project. Its records name the museum holding each tablet, which is where most of the institutions on this page come from. Its…

The Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative keeps the standard catalogue of cuneiform tablets wherever they are held. Its own pages ask not to be harvested, so only its published bulk dump was used, verified against the checksum it…
INSTITUTIONS THESE RECORDS NAME AS THE HOLDER
Where the objects themselves are. Most of these institutions publish nothing openly — they are named as the holder inside records from the collections above.

Half of the named objects reach us with no holder recorded anywhere in our sources, and nearly half of the photographs are among them. Several are famous enough that their museum is common knowledge — but common knowledge is not…
A museum we hold nothing from. The card says why, because the reason is almost never that the objects are not there.
The Netherlands' national museum, in Amsterdam.
03 / NAMED, BUT WITH NO PAGE HERE

The cuneiform catalogues record a holder for almost every tablet, and these 105 institutions and private collections are named among them. We hold catalogue rows about their objects, no photographs, and nothing fetched from the institutions themselves — so they have a line here rather than a page.
An object in a case is not an argument. It is where one can begin.

Built from this project's own research corpus, retrieved 2026-10-17. The most photographed collection here holds 43 of these pictures. Sources, licences and checksums are registered in the project's source register.
